caseTitle: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India
court: Supreme Court of India (9-Judge Constitution Bench)
holdingSummary: Right to privacy is a fundamental right protected under Article 21 and Part III of the Constitution. Foundational precedent for the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023.

caseTitle: Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India
court: Supreme Court of India (5-Judge Constitution Bench)
holdingSummary: Reads down Section 377 IPC to decriminalise consensual same-sex relations between adults; the provision was accordingly not reproduced in the BNS 2023.
Laid down guidelines for prevention of sexual harassment at the workplace, later codified by the POSH Act, 2013.

caseTitle: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
holdingSummary: Expanded Article 21 to require that any procedure depriving a person of life or liberty be fair, just and reasonable, and read Articles 14, 19 and 21 together.

caseTitle: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
holdingSummary: Established the Basic Structure Doctrine — Parliament's constituent power to amend the Constitution under Article 368 cannot alter its basic structure.

caseTitle: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar
holdingSummary: Directs police not to automatically arrest on a Section 498A IPC (now BNS s.85) complaint; mandates a Section 41/41A CrPC (now BNSS s.35) checklist before arrest. A Bihar-origin case directly relevant to the firm's home jurisdiction.

caseTitle: Lalita Kumari v. Govt. of U.P.
court: Supreme Court of India (5-Judge Constitution Bench)
holdingSummary: Registration of an FIR is mandatory under Section 154 CrPC (now BNSS s.173) if the information discloses a cognizable offence; preliminary inquiry is permitted only in specified categories.

caseTitle: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal
holdingSummary: Laid down binding guidelines on arrest and detention procedure to prevent custodial violence, later substantially incorporated into statute.

caseTitle: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India
holdingSummary: Struck down Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 as unconstitutional for vagueness and chilling effect on free speech.
